title: BlueQubit Selects Eight Teams for Quantum Flywheel Grant Programme
html:
Insider Brief

  • BlueQubit selected eight research teams from more than 160 proposals across 29 countries for its $150,000 Quantum Flywheel grant programme, supported by IBM, AWS and NVIDIA.
  • The selected teams will receive $10,000–$40,000 in AI and computing credits to work on quantum advantage, quantum error correction and classical simulation of quantum advantage claims.
  • Awardees will receive access to BlueQubit‘s platform, including AI-assisted circuit design, classical simulation and execution on IBM quantum computers, while 50 additional applicants will receive $300 in credits each.

PRESS RELASE — BlueQubit today announced the research teams selected for its Quantum Flywheel grant program, a $150,000 initiative created with support from IBM, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and NVIDIA Accelerated Computing. Awardees receive three months of credits for AI tokens and classical and quantum compute, with awards ranging from $10,000 to $40,000 per proposal.

Launched in September, Quantum Flywheel addresses a bottleneck in research: frontier AI tools let scientists draft experimental pipelines in hours, but hardware access still limits how quickly they can test those ideas. The program pairs AI-driven quantum circuit design with direct access to IBM quantum computers, NVIDIA GPU instances on AWS, and large-core CPU machines via BlueQubit’s platform.

The five-week open call drew more than 160 proposals from research groups in 29 countries, and eight teams were selected.

Four teams were selected in AI for quantum advantage on current quantum computers:

  • Ignacio Cirac of the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics
  • Tushar Pandey of Texas A&M University
  • Tobias Nadolny of ETH Zurich
  • Roberto dos Reis of Northwestern University

Three teams were selected in AI for quantum error correction:

  • Victor V. Albert of the Joint Center for Quantum Information and Computer Science (QuICS) at the University of Maryland
  • Oscar Humberto Montiel Ross of Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Centro de Investigación y Desarrollo de Tecnología Digital (CITEDI)
  • Davit Aghamalyan of the Singapore University of Technology and Design

One team was selected in AI for adversarial classical simulation of quantum advantage claims:

  • Xiaoyu Ouyang of the California Institute of Technology

In addition to the eight funded teams, BlueQubit will award $300 in compute and AI credits to 50 additional applicants.

“The response to Quantum Flywheel confirmed that researchers are ready to put frontier AI to work on the hardest problems in quantum computing,” said Hrant Gharibyan, CEO of BlueQubit. “These eight teams span algorithm discovery, error correction, and the adversarial classical work that keeps the field honest. We are excited to see what they build.”

Awardees gain access to BlueQubit’s AI-native quantum development platform, with end-to-end support from code generation and simulation to execution on IBM quantum computers. By combining AI-driven quantum circuit design with access to real quantum hardware, the platform enables researchers to explore new applications, advance fundamental quantum information science, and establish open, reproducible benchmarks for the global scientific community.

To learn more, visit https://www.bluequbit.io/quantum-flywheel.

Mohib Ur Rehman

MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE

BlueQubit specializes in quantum computing software, providing a cloud-based platform that enables enterprises, defense, and academic users to run advanced quantum algorithms on leading QPUs such as IBM Heron and Quantinuum H2. The company focuses on making quantum computing accessible for research and industry applications in finance, AI, and optimization. BlueQubit offers high-performance quantum simulators, SDK integration, and seamless migration from other quantum frameworks, supporting rapid prototyping and benchmarking. Its solutions address real-world challenges such as risk analysis, derivative pricing, and combinatorial optimization, emphasizing ease of use and practical value for early adopters.

IBM is an iconic technology pioneer founded in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company and officially renamed International Business Machines Corporation in 1924. Beyond foundational computing, IBM possesses a deep legacy in aerospace and defense from building the guidance computers and Instrument Unit for NASA's historic Apollo missions to partnering with Airbus on CIMON, the first AI assistant on the ISS.

NVIDIA Corporation is an American multinational technology company and a global player in accelerated computing and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Founded in 1993, the company pushes the aerospace frontier with the Space-1 Vera Rubin Module, a platform for orbital data centers that delivers massive AI-compute Space Computing. This NVIDIA technology enables satellites and autonomous spacecraft to process and fuse sensor data rapidly Space Computing.
